title: Learning Causal Networks from Episodic Data

problem.claim: Causal discovery from episodic observations must account for episode-specific sampling bias and possible changes in causal interactions.

gap.claim: Traditional causal discovery assumes a single observational dataset, which does not address episodic selection bias or changing causal interactions across episodes.

contributions.claim: A framework for causal modeling of episodic data is introduced using context switches and episodic selection bias.
Conditions are established under which information-theoretic scoring criteria can be applied for causal discovery while preserving consistency.
CONTINENT is proposed to discover causal models progressively online across episodes without re-learning the model for each new episode.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments across settings including selection bias, unknown interventions, and network changes report that CONTINENT works well in practice.
The authors report that CONTINENT outperforms the baselines by a clear margin.

narrative_sequence.summary: Real-world observations may arrive over time in episodes rather than as one batch.
Episodic data can involve biased samples and changing causal interactions, challenging single-dataset causal discovery.
The work introduces episodic causal modeling based on context switches and episodic selection bias.
It gives consistency conditions for information-theoretic scoring and proposes the online CONTINENT algorithm.
Experiments report practical performance and a clear margin over baselines across several settings.

source_observation.claim: Episodic data may combine selection bias with changes in causal interactions across episodes.

interpretation.claim: Causal discovery methods for evolving data should model both distributional selection effects and structural changes.

application.claim: Use an episodic causal modeling framework when observations arrive over time and episode conditions may differ.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the framework applies when episodes are unbiased and causally unchanged.

unknowns: Specific conditions for consistency are not provided.
Algorithmic details, datasets, metrics, and quantitative results are not provided.
The baselines and meaning of the reported clear margin are not specified.
